questions.question: The two vectors \([1, 1, 1]\) and \([1, a, a^2]\), where \(a = \left(-\dfrac{1}{2} + j\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\), are
questions.explanation:
Let the two given complex vectors be represented as row matrices \(X\) and \(Y\): \[X = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad Y = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \end{bmatrix}\] where \(a\) represents the complex cube root of unity: \[a = -\frac{1}{2} + j\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = e^{j\frac{2\pi}{3}}\] Its square \(a^2\) corresponds to its complex conjugate (\(a^*\)), given by: \[a^2 = -\frac{1}{2} - j\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{3}}\] \[X Y^{\top} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ a \\ a^2 \end{bmatrix} = 1 + a + a^2\] From the fundamental mathematical properties of the complex cube roots of unity, the sum of all three roots is identically zero: \[1 + a + a^2 = 0\] Since \(X Y^{\top} = 0\), the two vectors satisfy the condition for orthogonality. Now let us check if the vectors are normalized (i.e., whether they have a unit magnitude): \[X X^{\top} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = 1^2 + 1^2 + 1^2 = 3 \neq 1\] \[Y Y^{\mathsf{H}} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ a^* \\ (a^2)^* \end{bmatrix} = 1 \cdot 1 + a \cdot a^* + a^2 \cdot (a^2)^* = 1 + |a|^2 + |a|^4\] \[Y Y^{\mathsf{H}} = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 \neq 1\] Because the inner product equals zero but the lengths of the vectors are not equal to \(1\) (\(\|X\| = \|Y\| = \sqrt{3}\)), the vectors \(X\) and \(Y\) are orthogonal but not orthonormal. \[\boxed{\text{(B) Orthogonal}}\]
Key points
  • Properties of Cube Roots of Unity: For \(a = e^{j\frac{2\pi}{3}}\), the properties \(a^3 = 1\) and \(1 + a + a^2 = 0\) hold true.
  • Orthogonal vs. Orthonormal: Two vectors \(X\) and \(Y\) are orthogonal if their inner product equals zero. They are defined as orthonormal if they are orthogonal and each vector possesses a unit norm (\(\|X\| = 1\), \(\|Y\| = 1\)).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Inner Product Definition: In pure complex vector spaces, remember that the true inner product uses the conjugate transpose (\(\mathsf{H}\)), so \(\langle X, Y \rangle = X Y^{\mathsf{H}}\). In this specific problem, using either \(X Y^{\top}\) or \(X Y^{\mathsf{H}}\) evaluates to zero, but failing to include the conjugate when evaluating vector length (\(Y Y^{\top}\) instead of \(Y Y^{\mathsf{H}}\)) can lead to calculation errors.
  • Misinterpreting Orthogonality: Do not automatically assume that because a vector contains complex coefficients, its magnitude squared will include imaginary components. The norm squared (\(\|Y\|^2\)) is always a real scalar value.

questions.question: Roots of the algebraic equation \(x^3 + x^2 + x + 1 = 0\) are
questions.explanation:
Given the algebraic equation: \[x^3 + x^2 + x + 1 = 0\] We can solve for its roots by grouping the terms: \[x^2(x + 1) + 1(x + 1) = 0\] \[(x + 1)(x^2 + 1) = 0\] Equating each factor to zero:
  • For the first factor: \[x + 1 = 0 \implies x = -1\]
  • For the second factor: \[x^2 + 1 = 0 \implies x^2 = -1 \implies x = \pm \sqrt{-1}\] Using the imaginary unit symbol \(j\) (where \(j = \sqrt{-1}\)): \[x = j, -j\]
Thus, the roots of the equation are \((-1, j, -j)\). \[\boxed{\text{(d) } (-1, j, -j)}\]

questions.question: The function \(f(x) = 2x - x^2 + 3\) has
options: a maxima at \(x = 1\) and a minima at \(x = 5\)
a maxima at \(x = 1\) and a minima at \(x = -5\)
questions.explanation: Given the function: \[f(x) = 2x - x^2 + 3\] To find the critical points, we differentiate \(f(x)\) with respect to \(x\): \[f'(x) = \frac{d}{dx}(2x - x^2 + 3) = 2 - 2x\] Setting the first derivative to zero to find the stationary points: \[f'(x) = 0\] \[2 - 2x = 0 \implies 2x = 2 \implies x = 1\] To determine whether the function has a maximum or minimum at \(x = 1\), we evaluate the second derivative \(f''(x)\): \[f''(x) = \frac{d}{dx}(2 - 2x) = -2\] Since \(f''(1) = -2 < 0\), the function achieves a local maximum at \(x = 1\). Furthermore, because \(f(x) = -x^2 + 2x + 3\) represents a downward-opening parabola, this maximum is global, and there are no other extrema (minima) anywhere else on the real number line. Therefore, the function has only a maxima at \(x = 1\). \[\boxed{\text{(c)  only a maxima at } x = 1}\]

questions.explanation:
Given vectors \[\vec{v}_1=[1,1,1]\] and \[\vec{v}_2=[1,a,a^2]\] where \[a=-\frac{1}{2}+j\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\] Since \(a\) is a cube root of unity, \[1+a+a^2=0\] Now compute the dot product: \[\vec{v}_1 \cdot \vec{v}_2 = 1+a+a^2 = 0\] Hence, the two vectors are orthogonal. To be orthonormal, both vectors must also have unit magnitude, which is not true here. \[\boxed{\text{(b) Orthogonal}}\]
Key points
  • Cube roots of unity satisfy \[1+a+a^2=0\]
  • If the dot product of two vectors is zero, the vectors are orthogonal.
  • Orthonormal vectors must be both orthogonal and unit vectors.

questions.question: A point \(z\) has been plotted in the complex plane, as shown in figure below. The plot of the complex number \(y = \frac{1}{z}\) is
questions.explanation:
Let \(z = x + iy\). Given that \(z\) lies in the first quadrant of the unit circle: \[0 < x < 1, \quad 0 < y < 1\] \[0 < \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} < 1\] Now, consider the reciprocal function \(\frac{1}{z}\): \[\frac{1}{z} = \frac{1}{x + iy} = \frac{x - iy}{x^2 + y^2} = \left(\frac{x}{x^2 + y^2}\right) + i\left(\frac{-y}{x^2 + y^2}\right)\] Since \(x > 0\) and \(y > 0\): \[\frac{x}{x^2 + y^2} > 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{-y}{x^2 + y^2} < 0\] Since the real part is positive and the imaginary part is negative, \(\frac{1}{z}\) lies in the \(\text{IV}\) quadrant. Next, checking the magnitude of \(\frac{1}{z}\): \[\left| \frac{1}{z} \right| = \left| \frac{1}{x + iy} \right| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}}\] Given that \(0 < \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} < 1\), its reciprocal satisfies: \[\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}} > 1\] So, \(\frac{1}{z}\) lies outside the unit circle in the \(\text{IV}\) quadrant. \[\boxed{D}\]
Key points
  • Complex Inversion Mapping: The mapping \(w = \frac{1}{z}\) inverts the magnitude (\(\left|w\right| = \frac{1}{\left|z\right|}\)) and negates the argument (\(\arg(w) = -\arg(z)\)).
  • Quadrant Mapping: Points in the first quadrant (\(0 < \theta < \pi/2\)) map to the fourth quadrant (\(-\pi/2 < -\theta < 0\)) under inversion.
Mistakes to avoid
Note that if \(\left|z\right| < 1\), then \(\left|1/z\right| > 1\);the point does not remain inside the unit circle.

questions.question: A zero mean random signal is uniformly distributed between limits \(-a\) and \(+a\) and its mean square value is equal to its variance. Then the r.m.s value of the signal is
questions.explanation:
For a uniformly distributed random variable over the interval \[[-a,a]\] the mean is zero. Given that the mean square value is equal to the variance. Since mean is zero, \[\text{Variance} = E[X^2]\] Also, r.m.s. value is defined as \[X_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{E[X^2]}\] For a uniform distribution over \([-a,a]\), \[E[X^2]=\frac{a^2}{3}\] Hence, \[X_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{a^2}{3}}\] \[X_{\text{rms}}=\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}\] \[\boxed{\text{(a) }\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}}\]
Key points
  • For zero mean random variables: \[\text{Variance}=E[X^2]\]
  • r.m.s. value is: \[\sqrt{E[X^2]}\]

questions.question: The r.m.s value of the current i(t) in the circuit shown below is
questions.explanation:
Given the sinusoidal voltage source is \(v(t) = 1.0\sin(t)\,\text{V}\), the angular frequency is \(\omega = 1\,\text{rad/s}\). Representing each circuit element as an impedance in the phasor domain:
  • Impedance of the \(1\,\text{F}\) capacitor: \[Z_{C} = \frac{1}{j\omega C} = \frac{1}{j(1)(1)} = -j\,\Omega\]
  • Impedance of the \(1\,\text{H}\) inductor: \[Z_{L} = j\omega L = j(1)(1) = j\,\Omega\]
The total impedance of the top branch is the series combination of the inductor and the capacitor: \[Z_{top} = Z_{C} + Z_{L} = -j + j = 0\,\Omega\] Since the inductor and capacitor cancel the impedance of each other, the upper branch acts as a short circuit across the parallel \(1\,\Omega\) resistor. Because the \(1\,\Omega\) parallel resistor is shorted out by the upper branch, no current flows through it. The circuit simplifies to a single loop consisting of the remaining \(1\,\Omega\) series resistor and the alternating voltage source. The instantaneous current \(i(t)\) through the loop is: \[i(t) = \frac{1.0\sin(t)}{1} = 1.0\sin(t)\,\text{A}\] The peak value of the current is \(I_{m} = 1.0\,\text{A}\). Therefore, the RMS value of the current is calculated as: \[I_{rms} = \frac{I_{m}}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{(b)\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}A}\]

questions.question: The voltage applied to a circuit is \(100\sqrt{2}\cos(100\pi t)\) volts and the circuit draws a current of \(10\sqrt{2}\sin(100\pi t+\pi/4)\) amperes. Taking the voltage as the reference phasor, the phasor representation of the current in amperes is
questions.explanation:
Given the instantaneous voltage expression: \[v(t) = 100\sqrt{2}\cos(100\pi t)\,\text{V}\] The given instantaneous current expression is: \[i(t) = 10\sqrt{2}\sin\left(100\pi t + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\,\text{A}\] To compare the phases accurately, we must first convert the sine function into a cosine function using the identity \(\sin(\theta) = \cos\left(\theta - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\): \[i(t) = 10\sqrt{2}\cos\left(100\pi t + \frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\] \[i(t) = 10\sqrt{2}\cos\left(100\pi t - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\,\text{A}\] Taking the voltage \(v(t)\) as the reference phasor and comparing the two cosine expressions, the current lags the voltage by an angle of \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) radians. In phasor domain representation, using the root-mean-square (RMS) value for the magnitude: \[I = 10\angle -\frac{\pi}{4}\,\text{A}\]
Key points
  • When comparing the phase difference between two alternating quantities, both expressions must be converted into the same trigonometric form (either both sine or both cosine) with positive amplitudes.
  • The standard conversion form is \(\sin(\omega t) = \cos\left(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) or \(\cos(\omega t) = \sin\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).
  • Consider the RMS values.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not directly compare the phase angles while one function is in sine and the other is in cosine, as this leads to an incorrect phase difference.
\[\boxed{(b)10\angle-\pi/4}\]

questions.explanation:
The step response of an LTI system is obtained by convolving the impulse response with the unit step function: \[s(t)=h(t)*u(t).\] Given, \[h(t)=\left(e^{-t}+e^{-2t}\right)u(t).\] The step response is \[s(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\left(e^{-\tau}+e^{-2\tau}\right)d\tau.\] Evaluating the integral, \[\begin{aligned}
s(t)
&=\left(1-e^{-t}\right)
+\frac{1}{2}\left(1-e^{-2t}\right)\\
&=\frac{3}{2}-e^{-t}-\frac{1}{2}e^{-2t}.
\end{aligned}\] Hence, \[s(t)=\left(\frac{3}{2}-e^{-t}-\frac{1}{2}e^{-2t}\right)u(t).\] \[\boxed{\text{(c) }\left(1.5-e^{-t}-0.5e^{-2t}\right)u(t)}\]

questions.question: A low-pass filter with a cut-off frequency of \(30\text{ Hz}\) is cascaded with a high-pass filter with a cut-off frequency of \(20\text{ Hz}\). The resultant system of filters will function as
questions.explanation:
Cascaded Filter Analysis:
  • High-Pass Filter (HPF): Passes frequencies \(f \ge 20\,\text{Hz}\).
  • Low-Pass Filter (LPF): Passes frequencies \(f \le 30\,\text{Hz}\).
  • When cascaded, the overall frequency response is the intersection of both passbands: \[20\,\text{Hz} \le f \le 30\,\text{Hz}\]
Conclusion:
Since only a specific band of frequencies (\(20\,\text{Hz}\) to \(30\,\text{Hz}\)) is allowed to pass while frequencies below \(20\,\text{Hz}\) and above \(30\,\text{Hz}\) are attenuated, the resultant system functions as a band-pass filter. \[\boxed{\text{(D) a band-pass filter}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
Ensure that the HPF cut-off frequency is lower than the LPF cut-off frequency (\(f_L < f_H\)) to form a band-pass filter; if \(f_L > f_H\), no band of frequencies is passed in cascade.

questions.explanation:
Given data:
  1. DC current gain, \(\beta = 30\)
  2. Collector to base reverse saturation current, \(I_{CB0} \approx 0\text{ A}\)
  3. Diode forward voltage, \(V_{\gamma} = 0.7\text{ V}\)
  4. \(V_{BE} = 0.7\text{ V}\), \(V_{CE(\text{sat})} = 0.2\text{ V}\)
From the figure, the Zener diode is in the reverse breakdown region due to the \(-12\text{ V}\) voltage source. So, the Zener diode works as a \(5\text{ V}\) battery as shown below: Here, the P-terminal of the diode is at a higher potential than the N-terminal of the diode. Therefore, the diode and emitter junction \(J_E\) will be forward biased due to \(-12\text{ V}\). Hence, the BJT will be either in the active region or in the saturation region.
Method 1
Assuming the transistor is in the active region, \[V_{BE(\text{active})} = 0.7\text{ V}\] Applying KVL in loop (1): \[-5 + I_B \times 1 + 0.7 + 0.7 = 0\] \[I_B = 5 - 1.4 = 3.6\text{ mA}\] Collector current is given by: \[I_C = \beta I_B = 30 \times 3.6 = 108\text{ mA}\] Applying KVL in loop (2): \[0 + 2.2 I_C + V_{CE} - 12 = 0\] \[V_{CE} = 12 - 2.2 \times 108 = -225.6\text{ V}\] \[V_{CB} = V_{CE} - V_{BE} = -225.6 - 0.7 = -226.3\text{ V}\] From the above figure, it is clear that the collector of the given npn BJT is negatively biased and the base is positively biased; therefore, the collector-to-base junction is in forward bias. But in active mode, the collector-to-base junction must be reverse biased. Hence, our assumption is wrong. Therefore, the transistor is in the saturation region. Applying KVL in loop (2): \[2.2 I_{C(\text{sat})} + V_{CE(\text{sat})} - 12 = 0\] Assume \(V_{CE(\text{sat})} = 0.2\text{ V}\): \[2.2 I_{C(\text{sat})} + 0.2 - 12 = 0\] \[I_{C(\text{sat})} = 5.36\text{ mA}\] Hence, the correct option is (D).
Method 2
Assuming the transistor is in the saturation region: \[V_{BE(\text{sat})} = 0.7\text{ V}, \quad V_{CE(\text{sat})} = 0.2\text{ V}\] For a transistor to be in the saturation region: \[I_{B(\text{min})} \le I_B \implies \frac{I_{C(\text{sat})}}{\beta} \le I_B \quad \text{--- (i)}\] Applying KVL in loop (1): \[-5 + I_B \times 1 + 0.7 + 0.7 = 0\] \[I_B = 5 - 1.4 = 3.6\text{ mA} \quad \text{--- (ii)}\] Applying KVL in loop (2): \[0 + 2.2 I_{C(\text{sat})} + V_{CE(\text{sat})} - 12 = 0\] \[I_{C(\text{sat})} = \frac{12 - V_{CE(\text{sat})}}{2.2} = \frac{12 - 0.2}{2.2} = 5.36\text{ mA}\] Hence, \[I_{B(\text{min})} = \frac{I_{C(\text{sat})}}{\beta} = \frac{5.36 \times 10^{-3}}{30} = 1.78\text{ mA} \quad \text{--- (iii)}\] From equations (ii) and (iii): \[I_{B(\text{min})} < I_B \quad \text{--- (iv)}\] From equations (i) and (iv), the transistor satisfies the condition of saturation. Hence, our assumption is correct and the transistor is working in the saturation region.
Therefore, current through collector is given by: \[\boxed{I_{C(\text{sat})} = 5.36\text{ mA}}\]
Key points
  • Transistor operating region can be determined by checking the bias conditions of both the base-emitter and collector-base junctions.
  • For saturation, the base current must be greater than or equal to \(I_{B(\text{min})} = \frac{I_{C(\text{sat})}}{\beta}\).

questions.question: The steady-state error of a unity feedback linear system for a unit step input is \(0.1\). The steady-state error of the same system, for a pulse input \(r(t)\) having a magnitude of \(10\) and a duration of one second as shown in the figure is
questions.explanation:
Given a unity feedback linear system with an open-loop transfer function \(G(s)\) and \(H(s) = 1\). The error signal in the \(s\)-domain is expressed as: \[E(s) = \frac{R(s)}{1 + G(s)}\] Case 1: Unit Step Input
For a unit step input, \(r_1(t) = u(t) \implies R_1(s) = \dfrac{1}{s}\). The steady-state error \(e_{ss1}\) is given as \(0.1\): \[e_{ss1} = \lim_{s \to 0} s E(s) = \lim_{s \to 0} s \cdot \frac{1/s}{1 + G(s)} = 0.1\] \[\lim_{s \to 0} \frac{1}{1 + G(s)} = 0.1\] Case 2: Pulse Input
The input pulse of height \(10\) and duration \(1\,\text{s}\) is: \[r_2(t) = 10[u(t) - u(t - 1)]\] \[R_2(s) = \frac{10}{s}\left(1 - e^{-s}\right)\] The steady-state error \(e_{ss2}\) becomes: \[e_{ss2} = \lim_{s \to 0} s \cdot \frac{\dfrac{10}{s}\left(1 - e^{-s}\right)}{1 + G(s)}\] \[e_{ss2} = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{10\left(1 - e^{-s}\right)}{1 + G(s)}\] Substituting the boundary limit from Case 1 into the expression for Case 2: \[e_{ss2} = 10 \left(1 - e^{0}\right) \cdot \left[ \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{1}{1 + G(s)} \right] = 10 \cdot (1 - 1) \cdot 0.1 = 0\] \[\boxed{(A) \ \ 0}\]
Key points
Pulse Signals: A pulse of finite length possesses a total net area but drops completely back to zero value as \(t \to \infty\). Consequently, any stable linear system tracks it perfectly over long periods, yielding zero steady-state error.

questions.question: A two-loop position control system is shown below. The gain \(k\) of the Tacho-generator influences mainly the
options: phase shift of the closed loop transfer function at very low frequencies (\(\omega \to 0\))
phase shift of the closed loop transfer function at very high frequencies (\(\omega \to \infty\))
questions.explanation:
The overall system has unity negative feedback (\(H(s) = 1\)). The closed-loop characteristic equation is: \[1 + G_(s) \cdot 1 = 0\] \[1 + \frac{1}{s(s + 1 + k)} = 0\] \[s^2 + (1 + k)s + 1 = 0\] Comparing this to the standard second-order characteristic equation \(s^2 + 2\xi\omega_n s + \omega_n^2 = 0\): \[\omega_n^2 = 1 \implies \omega_n = 1\,\text{rad/s} \quad (\text{Constant, independent of } k)\] \[2\xi\omega_n = 1 + k \implies \xi = \frac{1 + k}{2}\] Since the peak overshoot is explicitly parameterized by the damping ratio via \(M_p = e^{-\frac{\xi\pi}{\sqrt{1 - \xi^2}}}\), varying the tacho-generator gain \(k\) alters \(\xi\) and thus mainly influences the peak overshoot. \[\boxed{\text{(A) peak overshoot}}\]
Key points
Tachometer Feedback: Tacho-generator feedback yields a derivative-like effect (\(k s\)), which introduces localized inner-loop damping to smooth out transient oscillations.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: An open loop system represented by the transfer func- tion \(G(s) = \dfrac{(s - 1)}{(s + 2)(s + 3)}\) is
options: stable and of the minimum phase type
stable and of the non-minimum phase type
unstable and of the minimum phase type
unstable and of the non-minimum phase type
questions.explanation:
To determine the nature of the open-loop system, we analyze its stability and its phase type based on the given transfer function: \[G(s) = \frac{s - 1}{(s + 2)(s + 3)}\] 1. Phase Type Analysis:
  • Poles: \(s = -2\) and \(s = -3\) (Both lie on the left-half of the \(s\)-plane).
  • Zeros: \(s = 1\) (Lies on the right-half of the \(s\)-plane).
  • Since there is a zero in the right-half of the \(s\)-plane (\(\text{RHS}\)), the system belongs to the non-minimum phase type.
2. Open-Loop Stability Analysis:
  • An open-loop system is stable if all its open-loop poles lie strictly in the left-half of the \(s\)-plane (\(\text{LHS}\)).
  • As both poles (\(s = -2, -3\)) have negative real parts, the open-loop system is completely stable.
\[\boxed{\text{(B) stable and of the non-minimum phase type}}\]
Key points
  • Minimum Phase System: A system is minimum-phase if all its poles and zeros lie in the left-half of the \(s\)-plane (excluding the \(j\omega\)-axis for zeros).
  • Non-Minimum Phase System: If any pole or zero lies in the right-half of the \(s\)-plane, it introduces additional phase lag and is classified as a non-minimum phase system.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: The open loop transfer function \(G(s)\) of a unity feedback control system is given as, \[G(s) = \frac{k\left(s + \dfrac{2}{3}\right)}{s^2(s + 2)}.\] From the root locus, it can be inferred that when \(k\) tends to positive infinity,
options: three roots with nearly equal real parts exist on the left half of the \(s\)-plane
one real root is found on the right half of the \(s\)-plane
the root loci cross the \(j\omega\) axis for a finite value of \(k\); \(k \neq 0\)
three real roots are found on the right half of the \(s\)-plane
questions.explanation:
The characteristic equation is defined by \(1 + G(s)H(s) = 0\): \[1 + \frac{K\left(s + \dfrac{2}{3}\right)}{s^2(s + 2)} = 0 \implies s^3 + 2s^2 + Ks + \frac{2K}{3} = 0\] RH Array:
\[\ \begin{array}{c|cc} s^3 & 1 & K \\ s^2 & 2 & \dfrac{2K}{3} \\ s^1 & \dfrac{2K - \dfrac{2K}{3}}{2} = \dfrac{2}{3}K \\ s^0 & \dfrac{2K}{3} \end{array}\] For any positive value of the open-loop gain (\(K > 0\)):
  • There are no sign changes in the first column of the Routh array.
  • Thus, the closed-loop system remains completely stable for all \(K > 0\).
  • Since no row can become entirely zero for \(K \neq 0\), the root loci never cross the \(j\omega\)-axis into the right-half plane.
Root Locus Construction:
  • Poles and Zeros: Number of poles \(P = 3\) (at \(s = 0, 0, -2\)), and number of zeros \(Z = 1\) (at \(s = -\dfrac{2}{3}\)).
  • Asymptotic Branches: \(P - Z = 3 - 1 = 2\) branches terminate at infinity.
  • Angle of Asymptotes: \[\theta = \frac{(2m + 1) \times 180^\circ}{P - Z} = 90^\circ \text{ and } 270^\circ\]
  • Centroid (\(\sigma\)): \[\sigma_{g} = \frac{\sum \text{Poles} - \sum \text{Zeros}}{P - Z} = \frac{(0 + 0 - 2) - \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}{2} = -\frac{2}{3}\]
As \(K \to \infty\), the two branches heading to infinity approach asymptotes centered at \(\text{Re}(s) = -\dfrac{2}{3}\), while the third branch terminates at the real zero \(s = -\dfrac{2}{3}\). Thus, all three roots share a nearly equal real part of \(-\dfrac{2}{3}\). \[\boxed{\text{(A) three roots with nearly equal real parts exist on the left half of the s-plane}}\]
Key points
The centroid \(\sigma\) dictates the intersection point of the asymptotes along the real axis of the \(s\)-plane.

questions.question: A \(220\,\text{V}\), DC shunt motor is operating at a speed of \(1440\,\text{rpm}\). The armature resistance is \(1.0\,\Omega\) and armature current is \(10\,\text{A}\). If the excitation of the machine is reduced by \(10\,\%\), the extra resistance to be put in the armature circuit to maintain the same speed and torque will be
questions.explanation: Since excitation of the machine is reduced by \(10\%\), the flux is also reduced by \(10\%\). \[E_{a} \propto \phi N\] Since speed is constant, \[E_{a} \propto \phi\] Also, \[T \propto \phi I_{a}\] Since torque is constant, \[I_{a} \propto \frac{1}{\phi}\] Initially, \[R_{a1}=1\,\Omega,\qquad I_{a1}=10\,\text{A}\] \[E_{a1}=V_{t}-I_{a1}R_{a1}\] \[E_{a1}=220-10\times1=210\,\text{V}\] Since flux is reduced by \(10\%\), \[\frac{E_{a2}}{E_{a1}}=\frac{\phi_{2}}{\phi_{1}}=0.9\] \[E_{a2}=0.9\times210=189\,\text{V}\] Also, \[\frac{I_{a2}}{I_{a1}}=\frac{\phi_{1}}{\phi_{2}}=\frac{1}{0.9}\] \[I_{a2}=\frac{10}{0.9}=11.11\,\text{A}\] Now, \[V_{t}=E_{a2}+I_{a2}R_{2}\] \[220=189+(11.11)R_{2}\] \[R_{2}=2.79\,\Omega\] Hence, external resistance added is \[R_{\text{ext}}=2.79-1=1.79\,\Omega\] \[\boxed{A}\]

questions.question: A three-phase \(440\,\text{V}\), \(6\) pole, \(50\,\text{Hz}\), squirrel cage induction motor is running at a slip of \(5\%\). The speed of stator magnetic field with respect to rotor magnetic field and speed of rotor with respect to stator magnetic field are
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Synchronous speed of the stator magnetic field is \[N_{s}=\frac{120f}{P}\] \[N_{s}=\frac{120\times 50}{6}=1000\,\text{rpm}\] Slip is given as \[s=5\%=0.05\] Rotor speed is \[N_{r}=N_{s}(1-s)\] \[N_{r}=1000(1-0.05)=950\,\text{rpm}\] The rotor magnetic field rotates with respect to rotor at slip speed, \[sN_{s}=0.05\times1000=50\,\text{rpm}\] Hence, speed of rotor magnetic field with respect to stator magnetic field is \[0\] because both rotate at synchronous speed with respect to stator. Speed of rotor with respect to stator magnetic field is \[N_{r}-N_{s}=950-1000=-50\,\text{rpm}\] So, no option is matching the final answer \[\boxed{*}\]
Key points
  • Stator magnetic field rotates at synchronous speed \(N_{s}\).
  • Rotor speed is \(N_{r}=N_{s}(1-s)\).
  • Rotor magnetic field also rotates at synchronous speed with respect to stator.
  • Therefore, relative speed between stator magnetic field and rotor magnetic field is zero.

questions.subject: electrical-machines
questions.question: A three-phase, salient pole synchronous motor is connected to an infinite bus. It is operated at no load at normal excitation. The field excitation of the motor is first reduced to zero and then increased in the reverse direction gradually. Then the armature current
options: first increases and then decreases steeply
first decreases and then increases steeply
questions.explanation: When a three-phase, salient pole synchronous motor is connected to an infinite bus and operated at no-load with normal excitation, the initial operating conditions are: \[E_f \approx V_t, \quad \delta \approx 0^\circ\] The armature current \(I_a\) is at its minimum absolute value (near zero). Phase 1: Reducing Excitation from Normal to Zero As the field excitation current \(I_f\) is gradually reduced to zero, the excitation voltage \(E_f\) decreases towards zero. To maintain the synchronous rotating magnetic field against the terminal voltage \(V_t\), the motor behaves as an under-excited machine and must draw a lagging reactive magnetizing current from the infinite bus. Therefore, the armature current \(I_a\) increases continuously. At exactly zero excitation (\(E_f = 0\)), the motor does not drop out of step because it is a salient pole machine. It continues to run at synchronous speed using reluctance torque alone: \[P = \frac{V_t^2}{2} \left( \frac{1}{X_q} - \frac{1}{X_d} \right) \sin(2\delta)\] To supply the tiny amount of active power required to overcome internal rotational and core losses, the power angle shifts to approximately \(\delta \approx -45^\circ\). Phase 2: Increasing Excitation in the Reverse Direction When the field current is reversed and gradually increased, it creates a magnetic field that directly opposes the stator's main field. Operating with a fully opposing negative field on the \(d\)-axis creates a highly unstable state. To find a lower-energy stable operating configuration, the rotor physically shifts relative to the stator field by \(180^\circ\) electrical (it slips a pole pitch). Due to this structural inversion, the reversed field excitation now aligns with and assists the stator's magnetic field instead of opposing it. Since the reversed field is now helping to magnetize the machine, the armature no longer needs to draw massive magnetizing current from the bus. Consequently, the armature current \(I_a\) decreases steeply. Thus, the armature current first increases and then decreases steeply. \[\boxed{\text{B}}\]

questions.explanation:
The converter is used to feed power from the DC side to the AC side. Hence, the converter operates as a line-commutated inverter. For a three-phase fully controlled bridge converter, \[V_{o}=\frac{3V_{ml}}{\pi}\cos\alpha\] For inverter operation, \[\alpha>90^\circ\] and the average output voltage must be negative. The current through the battery is \[I_{o}=\frac{V_{o}-(-400)}{R} =\frac{V_{o}+400}{R}\] For maximum current, \(V_{o}\) should have the minimum negative value. Key points
  • In line-commutated inverter operation, the converter transfers power from DC side to AC side.
  • For inversion, the firing angle must satisfy \(\alpha>90^\circ\).
  • Thyristor current direction cannot reverse, so voltage polarity must reverse for power reversal.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
  • (i) The compensating coil of a low power factor wattmeter compensates the effect of the impedance of the current coil.
  • (ii) The compensating coil of a low power factor wattmeter compensates the effect of the impedance of the voltage coil circuit.
questions.explanation:
In a Low Power Factor (LPF) wattmeter, errors become significant because the pressure (voltage) coil circuit has inductance. [figure unavailable] Hence pressure coil current \(I_p\) does not remain exactly in phase with the applied voltage. The pressure coil impedance is: \[Z_p=R_p+jX_p\] Thus, \(I_p\) lags the applied voltage, causing error in wattmeter reading, especially at low power factor. To reduce this error, a compensating coil is used. The compensating coil: i) is connected in series with the pressure coil circuit, ii) carries pressure coil current \(I_p\), iii) is wound coaxially over the main current coil, iv) produces magnetic field opposite to the unwanted field due to pressure coil current. Hence, \[\text{Current coil field}\propto (I+I_p)\] \[\text{Compensating coil field} \propto I_p\] and acts in opposition. Therefore, net field becomes: \[(I+I_p)-I_p=I\] Thus, the resultant field depends only on the load current \(I\). Hence, the error due to pressure coil current is neutralized. Therefore, the compensating coil compensates the effect of: \[\text{Pressure (voltage) coil circuit impedance}\] and not the impedance of the current coil. Statement (i):
``The compensating coil compensates the effect of impedance of the current coil.'' This is false, because the compensating coil does not compensate current coil impedance. \[\boxed{(i)\ \text{False}}\] Statement (ii):
``The compensating coil compensates the effect of impedance of the voltage coil circuit.'' This is true, because it neutralizes the phase error caused by: \[R_p+jX_p\] \[\boxed{(ii)\ \text{True}}\] Therefore, the correct option is \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }\text{(i) is False but (ii) is True}}\]

questions.question: In order to develop to full potential, a baby needs to be physically able to respond to the environment. It can be inferred from the passage that
options: Full physical potential is needed in order for a baby to be able to respond to the environment.
It is necessary for a baby to be able to physically respond to the environment for it to develop its full potential.
Response to the environment of physically able babies needs to be developed to its full potential.
A physically able baby needs to develop its full potential in order to respond to its environment.
questions.explanation:
Let us break down the exact logical proposition structure presented in the prompt:
  • Premise: "In order to develop to full potential, a baby needs to be physically able to respond to the environment."
  • This follows the classical conditional requirement format: \(A\) is necessary for \(B\) (\(B \implies A\)).
  • Therefore, being physically able to respond to the environment (\(A\)) is an essential requirement or a necessary condition for a baby to achieve its full potential (\(B\)).
Evaluating the choices:
  • Option A: Inverts the logic by claiming full potential is needed to respond, which is structurally backwards.
  • Option B: Correctly restates the premise using explicit logical constraints: it clarifies that responding to the environment is a necessary condition for developing full potential.
  • Option C and Option D: Warp the conditional links by converting necessary conditions into absolute sufficient statements.
\[\boxed{\text{B: It is necessary for a baby to be able to physically respond to the environment for it to develop its full potential.}}\]
Key points
  • Necessary Conditions vs Sufficient Conditions: The structural qualifier phrase "In order to achieve X, Y is required" frames Y as an indispensable necessity. It does not mean Y alone is automatically sufficient to guarantee X, but without Y, X cannot occur.

questions.question: If \(m\) students require a total of \(m\) pages of stationery in \(m\) days, then 100 students will require 100 pages of stationery in
questions.explanation:
We can solve this problem using the unitary method by evaluating the rate of resource consumption per student. Step 1: Understand the baseline rate data
Given that \(m\) students require a total of \(m\) pages of stationery over a span of \(m\) days, the work rate formula is: \[\text{Pages required} \propto \text{Number of students} \times \text{Number of days}\] \[\text{Pages} = k \times \text{Students} \times \text{Days}\] Using the initial parameters to find the constant \(k\): \[m = k \times m \times m \implies k = \dfrac{1}{m}\] Step 2: Apply the rate constant to the new scenario Let \(D\) be the number of days required by \(100\) students to use \(100\) pages of stationery: \[100 = \left(\dfrac{1}{m}\right) \times 100 \times D\] \[100 = \dfrac{100D}{m} \implies D = m \text{ days}\] \[\boxed{\text{D: } m \text{ days}}\]
Key points
  • Joint Variation Rate Layouts: Time required is directly proportional to the total workload (pages) and inversely proportional to the operating workforce size (students): \[\dfrac{\text{Students}_1 \times \text{Days}_1}{\text{Pages}_1} = \dfrac{\text{Students}_2 \times \text{Days}_2}{\text{Pages}_2}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not blindly jump to an option like "100 days" due to superficial pattern matching with the numerical constants; always process the underlying inverse time mechanics.

questions.question:
The number of solutions for the following system of inequalities is \[\begin{aligned}
        X_1 &\ge 0 \\
        X_2 &\ge 0 \\
        X_1 + X_2 &\le 10 \\
        2X_1 + 2X_2 &\ge 22
    \end{aligned}\]
questions.explanation:
We are given a system of linear inequalities with variables bounded in the first quadrant: \[\begin{aligned} 1) \quad &X_1 \ge 0 \\ 2) \quad &X_2 \ge 0 \\ 3) \quad &X_1 + X_2 \le 10 \\ 4) \quad &2X_1 + 2X_2 \ge 22 \implies 2(X_1 + X_2) \ge 22 \implies X_1 + X_2 \ge 11 \end{aligned}\] Let us evaluate inequalities (3) and (4) simultaneously:
  • Inequality (3) bounds the sum to a maximum ceiling of 10: \(X_1 + X_2 \le 10\).
  • Inequality (4) demands that the sum must be at least 11: \(X_1 + X_2 \ge 11\).
Since a real number value cannot be simultaneously less than or equal to 10 while being greater than or equal to 11 (\(11 \le X_1 + X_2 \le 10\)), these constraints are mutually exclusive. No overlapping feasibility region exists. Therefore, the number of solutions for the system is exactly 0. \[\boxed{\text{A: 0}}\]
Key points
  • Feasible Region Nullity: In linear programming models, if two constraint half-spaces display parallel boundary thresholds facing in opposite directions without overlap, the solution set is null.

  • \(n(C) = 200\) (Students taking C600)
  • \(n(E) = 60\) (Students taking E600)
Every single student is required to take at least one subject, meaning the union of the sets equals the entire class size: \[n(M \cup C \cup E) = N = 300\] Using the standard set inclusion-exclusion principle expansion for three sets: \[n(M \cup C \cup E) = n(M) + n(C) + n(E) - [n(M \cap C) + n(C \cap E) + n(M \cap E)] + n(M \cap C \cap E)\] Substitute the known values into the equation: \[300 = 100 + 200 + 60 - \sum n(\text{Pairs}) + n(M \cap C \cap E)\] \[300 = 360 - \sum n(\text{Pairs}) + n(M \cap C \cap E)\] \[\sum n(\text{Pairs}) - n(M \cap C \cap E) = 60 \quad \text{--- (1)}\] To find the *maximum possible value* of students taking all three subjects, let \(x = n(M \cap C \cap E)\). We rewrite equation (1) as: \[\sum n(\text{Pairs}) = 60 + x\] By principle bounding constraints, any student counted in all three subjects is inherently counted within each of the individual overlapping pairs: \[n(M \cap C) \ge x, \quad n(C \cap E) \ge x, \quad n(M \cap E) \ge x \implies \sum n(\text{Pairs}) \ge 3x\] Substitute our equation link into this inequality constraint: \[\begin{aligned} 60 + x &\ge 3x \\ 60 &\ge 2x \\ x &\le 30 \end{aligned}\] Thus, the maximum possible number of students who have taken all three subjects is 30. \[\boxed{\text{B: 30}}\]
Key points
  • Set Intersection Optimization: Maximizing the primary triple intersection region requires minimizing structural waste across individual non-overlapping dual-set pairs down to their baseline limits.

questions.question: Three sisters (R, S, and T) received a total of 24 toys during Christmas. The toys were initially divided among them in a certain proportion. Subsequently, R gave some toys to S which doubled the share of S. Then S in turn gave some of her toys to T, which doubled T's share. Next, some of T's toys were given to R, which doubled the number of toys that R currently had. As a result of all such exchanges, the three sisters were left with equal number of toys. How many toys did R have originally?
questions.explanation:
Let the number of toys originally held by sisters R, S, and T be represented by variables \(r, s,\) and \(t\) respectively. The absolute total number of toys is constant throughout all steps: \[r + s + t = 24 \text{ toys}\] At the end of all transactions, the three sisters are left with an equal number of toys: \[\text{Final toys per sister} = \dfrac{24}{3} = 8 \text{ toys}\] We solve this problem by working backwards step-by-step from the final state:
  • End State: \([R, S, T] = [8, 8, 8]\)
  • Reverse Step 3 (T doubled R's toys): R had \(8 \div 2 = 4\) toys. T gave away 4, so T had \(8 + 4 = 12\) toys. State: \([4, 8, 12]\)
  • Reverse Step 2 (S doubled T's toys): T had \(12 \div 2 = 6\) toys. S gave away 6, so S had \(8 + 6 = 14\) toys. State: \([4, 14, 6]\)
  • Reverse Step 1 (R doubled S's toys): S had \(14 \div 2 = 7\) toys. R gave away 7, so R had \(4 + 7 = 11\) toys. State: \([11, 7, 6]\)
Thus, R originally had exactly 11 toys. \[\boxed{\text{C: 11}}\]
Key points
  • Inversion Analysis: Finite transactional loops where cumulative volume remains constant are solved fastest by starting at the final equilibrium state and applying inverse arithmetic operations.

questions.explanation:
We need to distribute 3 distinct scholarships among 4 applicants, where any applicant can receive any number of scholarships. Step 1: Analyze the independent distribution choices

  • Scholarship 3 can be awarded to any of the 4 applicants (4 options).

questions.question: If \((2y+1)/(y+2) < 1\), then which of the following alternatives gives the CORRECT range of \(y\)?
questions.explanation:
Given the rational inequality expression: \[\dfrac{2y + 1}{y + 2} < 1\] Step 1: Rearrange the inequality to compare with zero Subtract 1 from both sides: \[\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2y + 1}{y + 2} - 1 &< 0 \\[1.5ex] \dfrac{(2y + 1) - (y + 2)}{y + 2} &< 0 \\[1.5ex] \dfrac{y - 1}{y + 2} &< 0 \end{aligned}\] Step 2: Find critical points and analyze intervals The critical boundary roots where the numerator or denominator equals zero are: \[y = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad y = -2\] Using the sign chart method (wavy curve method) across the partitioned intervals:
  • For \(y > 1\): Both \((y-1) > 0\) and \((y+2) > 0 \implies \text{Positive } (+)\)
  • For \(-2 < y < 1\): \((y-1) < 0\) but \((y+2) > 0 \implies \text{Negative } (-)\)
  • For \(y < -2\): Both \((y-1) < 0\) and \((y+2) < 0 \implies \text{Positive } (+)\)
Since we require the expression to be strictly less than zero (\(< 0\)), the valid interval is \(-2 < y < 1\). \[\boxed{\text{B: } -2 < y < 1}\]
Key points
  • Rational Inequalities Rule: Never cross-multiply by variable terms like \((y + 2)\) across an inequality sign, as the variable's sign is unknown and could reverse the inequality direction. Always transfer all terms to one side.

questions.question: A student attempted to solve a quadratic equation in \(x\) twice. However, in the first attempt, he incorrectly wrote the constant term and ended up with the roots as \((4, 3)\). In the second attempt, he incorrectly wrote down the coefficient of \(x\) and got the roots as \((3, 2)\). Based on the above information, the roots of the correct quadratic equation are
questions.explanation:
Let the correct quadratic equation format be \(x^2 + bx + c = 0\). Step 1: Extract valid parameters from the first attempt
In the first attempt, the student incorrectly wrote the constant term (\(c\)) but copied the coefficient of \(x\) (\(b\)) correctly.
  • Given roots: \((4,3)\)
  • The sum of the roots relates directly to \(b\): \[\text{Sum} = 4 + 3 = 7 = -b \implies b = -7\]
Step 2: Extract valid parameters from the second attempt
In the second attempt, the student incorrectly wrote the coefficient of \(x\) (\(b\)) but copied the constant term (\(c\)) correctly.
  • Given roots: \((3,2)\)
  • The product of the roots relates directly to \(c\): \[\text{Product} = 3 \times 2 = 6 = c \implies c = 6\]
Step 3: Construct the correct equation and find its true roots
Combining the true coefficients yields the original quadratic equation: \[x^2 - 7x + 6 = 0\] Factorizing by splitting the middle term: \[\begin{aligned} x^2 - 6x - x + 6 &= 0 \\ x(x - 6) - 1(x - 6) &= 0 \\ (x - 6)(x - 1) &= 0 \implies x = 6 \quad \text{or} \quad x = 1 \end{aligned}\] The actual roots of the correct quadratic equation are \((6,1)\). \[\boxed{\text{C: (6, 1)}}\]
Key points
  • Vieta's Formulas: For any quadratic equation \(x^2 + bx + c = 0\) with roots \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), the roots directly satisfy: \[\alpha + \beta = -b \quad \text{and} \quad \alpha\beta = c\]

questions.question: The variable cost (\(V\)) of manufacturing a product varies according to the equation \(V = 4q\), where \(q\) is the quantity produced. The fixed cost (\(F\)) of production of same product reduces with \(q\) according to the equation \(F = 100/q\). How many units should be produced to minimize the total cost (\(V+F\))?
questions.explanation:
We are given equations for variable cost \(V\) and fixed cost \(F\) relative to production quantity \(q\): \[V = 4q \quad \text{and} \quad F = \dfrac{100}{q}\] The total cost function \(C(q)\) is the sum of variable cost and fixed cost: \[C(q) = V + F = 4q + \dfrac{100}{q}\] Step 1: Differentiate with respect to production quantity \(q\)
To locate the production volume that minimizes total cost, take the first derivative and set it to zero: \[\dfrac{dC}{dq} = 4 - \dfrac{100}{q^2} = 0\] \[4 = \dfrac{100}{q^2} \implies 4q^2 = 100 \implies q^2 = 25 \implies q = 5 \quad (\text{since } q > 0)\] Step 2: Confirm the minimum with the second derivative
\[\dfrac{d^2C}{dq^2} = \dfrac{200}{q^3}\] Evaluating at \(q = 5\) yields \(\dfrac{200}{125} = 1.6 > 0\). Since the second derivative is positive, \(q = 5\) successfully minimizes total production cost. \[\boxed{\text{A: 5}}\]
Key points
  • Cost Optimization Minimums: Total cost optimizations can be solved dynamically by identifying where the marginal variable cost balances the changing marginal fixed asset costs.

questions.question: There are two candidates P and Q in an election. During the campaign, 40% of the voters promised to vote for P, and the rest for Q. However, on the day of election 15% of the voters went back on their promise to vote for P and instead voted for Q. 25% of the voters went back on their promise to vote for Q and instead voted for P. Suppose, P lost by 2 votes, then what was the total number of voters?
questions.explanation:
Let the total number of voters in the election be \(V\). Step 1: Set up the baseline campaign expectations
  • Promised votes for candidate P = \(40\%\) of \(V = 0.40V\)
  • Promised votes for candidate Q = Rest of the voters = \(60\%\) of \(V = 0.60V\)
Step 2: Account for the voting shifts on election day
  • \(15\%\) of P's promised voters switched to Q: \[\text{Loss for P} = 0.15 \times 0.40V = 0.06V\]
  • \(25\%\) of Q's promised voters switched to P: \[\text{Loss for Q} = 0.25 \times 0.60V = 0.15V\]
Step 3: Calculate final vote tally per candidate
\[\begin{aligned} \text{Final Votes for P} &= \text{Initial P} - \text{Switched from P} + \text{Switched from Q} \\ &= 0.40V - 0.06V + 0.15V = 0.49V \\[1.5ex] \text{Final Votes for Q} &= \text{Initial Q} - \text{Switched from Q} + \text{Switched from P} \\ &= 0.60V - 0.15V + 0.06V = 0.51V \end{aligned}\] Step 4: Solve for \(V\) using the margin constraint
We are given that candidate P lost by exactly 2 votes: \[\begin{aligned} \text{Votes for Q} - \text{Votes for P} &= 2 \\ 0.51V - 0.49V &= 2 \\ 0.02V &= 2 \\ V &= \dfrac{2}{0.02} = 100 \text{ voters} \end{aligned}\] \[\boxed{\text{A: 100}}\]
Key points
  • Double Shift Tracking: When modeling voter migration between two options, ensure that any volume deducted from one pool is explicitly added to the opposing pool to maintain total population integrity.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not misapply percentages by treating the \(15\%\) and \(25\%\) shifts as fractions of the global voter population \(V\); they are percentages of each candidate's local pool.

questions.question: Given that \(f(y) = |y| / y\), and \(q\) is any non-zero real number, the value of \(|f(q) - f(-q)|\) is
questions.explanation:
We are given the signum-style function definition: \[f(y) = \dfrac{|y|}{y}\] For any non-zero real number \(y\), the value of this function behaves as follows:
  • If \(y > 0\): \(f(y) = \frac{y}{y} = 1\)
  • If \(y < 0\): \(f(y) = \frac{-y}{y} = -1\)
We need to compute the absolute value expression for a non-zero real number \(q\): \[\text{Target} = |f(q) - f(-q)|\] Let us analyze the two possible cases for the sign of variable \(q\): Case 1: Assume \(q\) is positive (\(q > 0\))
If \(q > 0\), then \(-q < 0\). Evaluating our function values: \[f(q) = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad f(-q) = -1\] Substitute these values into our absolute target function: \[\text{Target} = |1 - (-1)| = |1 + 1| = |2| = 2\] Case 2: Assume \(q\) is negative (\(q < 0\))
If \(q < 0\), then \(-q > 0\). Evaluating our function values: \[f(q) = -1 \quad \text{and} \quad f(-q) = 1\] Substitute these values into our absolute target function: \[\text{Target} = |-1 - 1| = |-2| = 2\] In all possible cases, the expression evaluates to exactly 2. \[\boxed{\text{D: 2}}\]
Key points
  • Signum Function Properties: The function \(f(y) = \frac{|y|}{y}\) outputs the structural orientation sign of its input variable. Because \(q\) and \(-q\) must possess opposite signs, their corresponding function outputs are always pairs of \((1, -1)\) or \((-1, 1)\).

questions.question: The sum of \(n\) terms of the series \(4 + 44 + 444 + \dots\) is
questions.explanation:
We want to find the sum of \(n\) terms of the following arithmetic-geometric series: \[S_n = 4 + 44 + 444 + 4444 + \dots + \underbrace{444\dots4}_{n \text{ digits}}\] Step 1: Factor out the common digit 4
\[S_n = 4 \Big[ 1 + 11 + 111 + 1111 + \dots + \text{(term up to } n \text{ digits)} \Big]\] Step 2: Multiply and divide by 9 to create base-10 links
\[S_n = \dfrac{4}{9} \Big[ 9 + 99 + 999 + 9999 + \dots + \text{(term up to } n \text{ digits)} \Big]\] Step 3: Express each term as a power of 10 \[\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{4}{9} \Big[ (10^1 - 1) + (10^2 - 1) + (10^3 - 1) + \dots + (10^n - 1) \Big] \\[1.5ex] &= \dfrac{4}{9} \bigg[ \Big( 10^1 + 10^2 + 10^3 + \dots + 10^n \Big) - \Big( 1 + 1 + 1 + \dots + 1 \text{ ($n$ times)} \Big) \bigg] \end{aligned}\] Step 4: Sum the Geometric Progression (GP) series The first part forms a geometric progression with first term \(a = 10\) and common ratio \(r = 10\): \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} 10^i = \dfrac{10(10^n - 1)}{10 - 1} = \dfrac{10^{n+1} - 10}{9}\] Substitute this expression back into our equation: \[\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{4}{9} \left[ \dfrac{10^{n+1} - 10}{9} - n \right] \\[1.5ex] &= \dfrac{4}{9} \left[ \dfrac{10^{n+1} - 10 - 9n}{9} \right] \\[1.5ex] &= \dfrac{4}{81} \left[ 10^{n+1} - 9n - 10 \right] \end{aligned}\] This result matches the formulation presented in Option C. \[\boxed{\text{C: } \dfrac{4}{81}[10^{n+1} - 9n - 10]}\]
Key points
  • Uniform Digit Series Expansion: Any repeating single-digit series of value \(d\) can be systematically transformed into a base-10 geometric progression using the following multiplier: \[\dfrac{d}{9}(10^k - 1)\]
